state.misconception_label: Does not know the properties of a rectangle

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The angles highlighted on this rectangle with different length sides can never be... ![A rectangle with the diagonals drawn in. The angle on the right hand side at the centre is highlighted in red and the angle at the bottom at the centre is highlighted in yellow.](). I got acute because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about a rectangle like a table — the corners where the legs meet the top are always right angles, right? So just like how all table corners are right angles, all angles in a rectangle are equal. So if you see different angles in a rectangle, it's not a rectangle anymore. Imagine you were doing this with everyday objects you can see and touch — would your method still give the right answer?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I get what you're saying about the right angles, but I thought rectangles could have different lengths for the sides and still be the same shape. So, if the angles are always right angles, does that mean they can’t ever be acute like I thought? What if I draw a rectangle with really long sides and really short sides? Would that change anything?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a rectangle made out of different materials — like a wooden table with different lengths for the legs. Even if the sides are different lengths, the corners where the legs meet the top are always right angles. So, no matter how long or short the sides are, the angles will always be right angles. Imagine you were doing this with everyday objects you can see and touch — would your method still give the right answer?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now. So even if the sides of the rectangle are different lengths, the angles are always right angles, which means they can't be acute. But what if I draw a shape that looks like a rectangle but has angles that aren't right? Is that still a rectangle or something else?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly uses everyday analogies but never addresses the actual misconception about the angles formed by diagonals at the center of the rectangle (which can indeed be acute), instead discussing only corner angles, while the student shows confusion but no clear resolution of the original problem.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds every explanation in concrete, tangible real-world analogies (tables, wooden furniture, physical objects) and repeatedly encourages the student to connect abstract geometric concepts to everyday objects they can see and touch.
